title: How do you do case interview maths out loud without panicking?
description: The arithmetic is simple; doing it out loud under pressure is not. Approach first, round smartly, sanity-check everything.
hook: You do case maths out loud without panicking by following the same routine every time: say the approach, write the numbers down with units, calculate in small steps while you talk, check the size of the answer and say what it means. The maths itself is rarely hard: percentages, growth, margins and big numbers. The pressure comes from doing it while someone watches, and a routine is what takes that pressure away.
body:
In this guide

  • Why case maths feels harder than it is
  • Step 1: say the approach before the arithmetic
  • Step 2: write the numbers down with units
  • Step 3: make the arithmetic small
  • Step 4: talk while you calculate, then sanity-check
  • Step 5: say what the number means
  • A worked example: break-even, done well
  • What to do when you make a mistake
  • Common mistakes
  • Check yourself
  • Where to practise next

Why case maths feels harder than it is

The sums in a case are the kind you could do easily at a kitchen table. What changes in the interview is that you are thinking, writing and speaking at the same time, someone is judging you, and a wrong number seems as if it could end the case. That combination makes simple arithmetic feel fragile.

The interviewer is testing three things: can you set up the right calculation, can you get the number right without fuss, and can you turn it into a business conclusion. The routine below covers all three. Practise it until it is automatic, so that under pressure you follow habit rather than nerves.

Step 1: say the approach before the arithmetic

Before you touch a number, say what you are going to calculate and how:

"Profit from the new line is units times contribution per unit, minus the fixed launch cost. Does that make sense?"

Getting agreement first does two things. It catches a wrong set-up before you spend two minutes on it. And if you then slip on the arithmetic, the interviewer has already seen that your logic was right. Accuracy still counts, so this is a safety net, not an excuse.

Step 2: write the numbers down with units

Write each input neatly in a column, with its unit next to it: "250,000 customers", "$12 per customer per month". Units are your cheapest error check. A company with 250,000 subscribers at $12 a month earns 250,000 × $12 × 12 months = $36M a year. Writing "per month" next to the $12 is what reminds you of the final × 12, and forgetting it is one of the easiest ways to be out by an order of magnitude.

Units also stop you mixing a flow with a stock. If churn is 2% a month, the business loses about 5,000 of those 250,000 customers in the first month (before new joiners). That does not mean it loses 24% a year: churn compounds on a shrinking base, and 0.98¹² = 0.785, so about 21.5% of the starting customers leave within the year.

Step 3: make the arithmetic small

  • Percentages: build from 10%, 5% and 1%. 17% of 340: 10% is 34, 1% is 3.4, so 7% is 23.8. Total 57.8. See percentages in your head.
  • Big numbers: separate the digits from the zeros. 3.5M × 240: 3.5 × 24 = 84, then add back seven zeros (six from the million, one from 240) to get 840M. See multiplying big numbers.
  • Division: cancel zeros first. $4.5B ÷ 1.5M = 4,500 ÷ 1.5 = $3,000.
  • Growth: use the rule of 72. At 10% a year, something doubles in about 7 years. See the rule of 72.
  • Rounding: round to make the maths easy, and say so. "I'll treat 252,000 as a quarter of a million for a first pass" is transparent and costs under 1% of accuracy. Silently swapping a number looks careless. Do not round away the answer: 5.5B is not 5B.

All the formulas and shortcuts are on one page in the case maths cheat sheet. Profit, margin vs markup, contribution, break-even, payback, ROI, CAGR and a simple perpetuity come up in almost every case, so know those cold.

Step 4: talk while you calculate, then sanity-check

Calculate out loud at a steady pace. You do not need to narrate every carry, but say each intermediate result: "so contribution is 80 cents... times 15 million...". This lets the interviewer follow and catch a slip early, which is far better than discovering it at the end.

When you have a result, check its size against something you already know. Multiply back, compare with total revenue, or ask whether the answer is plausible:

"So about $1.5M a year. That's roughly 15% of their profit, which sounds plausible for a price change."

Step 5: say what the number means

A number without a so-what is half an answer. Every calculation should end with a sentence that links it to the client's decision and, ideally, proposes the next step. "So the new line pays back in three years, inside their four-year target. I'd now check whether the volume assumption holds." So-what thinking covers how to turn any number into an insight.

A worked example: break-even, done well

Question: A snack company spends $12M to launch a protein bar that sells for $1.50 with a variable cost of $0.70. How many bars does it need to sell to break even? It expects to sell 5M bars a year.

A strong answer:

"Break-even is the fixed cost divided by contribution per bar. Contribution is $1.50 minus $0.70, so 80 cents. $12M divided by 0.8 is 15M bars. Check: 15M times 80 cents is $12M. At 5M bars a year, that's three years to recover the launch cost. Before I'd call that attractive, I'd want to know the client's payback target and whether 5M bars a year is realistic for this market."

A weak answer:

"Er, 12 divided by... 1.50 minus 0.70... so 0.8... 15. Fifteen million?"

Both get the right number. Only the first shows the formula, a check, the payback and a next step. That is the difference between passing the maths and impressing with it.

What to do when you make a mistake

Everyone slips eventually. What matters is how you recover.

  • If you spot it yourself, say so plainly: "Sorry, I dropped a zero there. It's $840M, not $84M." Then carry on. Do not apologise twice.
  • If the interviewer questions a number, treat it as a hint, not an attack. Recheck the step aloud rather than defending the answer.
  • If you freeze, go back to the formula and restate it. Saying "revenue is customers times spend per customer" usually restarts the arithmetic.
  • If a sum is genuinely awkward, ask: "Would you mind if I round 37 to 40 to keep it simple?" Sensible rounding that you announce is part of good case maths, not a shortcut to hide.

For nerves more generally, read staying calm when nerves hit.

Common mistakes

  • Calculating before agreeing the approach, then discovering the set-up was wrong.
  • Dropping a unit: a monthly price never multiplied by 12, thousands added to millions.
  • Adding growth rates instead of multiplying them: three years at 10% is +33%, not +30%.
  • Mixing up margin and markup. See margin vs markup.
  • Stopping at the number without saying what it means for the client.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer.

1. What is 15% of 480?

  • 62
  • 72
  • 82
Show the answer

72. 10% = 48, 5% = 24, total 72.

2. Fixed costs $3M, price $25, variable cost $10. What is break-even volume?

  • 120,000
  • 200,000
  • 300,000
Show the answer

200,000. Contribution = $15. $3M ÷ $15 = 200,000 units.

3. Cost $80, price $100. Which is true?

  • Margin 25%, markup 20%
  • Margin 20%, markup 25%
  • Both 20%
Show the answer

Margin 20%, markup 25%. Margin is on price (20 ÷ 100); markup is on cost (20 ÷ 80).

4. Try it out loud: a factory makes 2.4M units a year running at 75% of capacity. How many extra units could it make at 90%, and what are they worth at $3 contribution each?

Give yourself 60 seconds.

Show a strong answer

"Full capacity is 2.4M ÷ 0.75 = 3.2M units. At 90% that's 2.88M, so 0.48M extra units. At $3 each, that's $1.44M a year of extra contribution. Check: 15 percentage points of 3.2M is 0.48M. So before building new capacity, the client could find about $1.4M a year from running the existing plant harder, if there is demand for the extra units."
